claim: ASIC1a is a proton-gated sodium channel involved in modulation of pain, fear, addiction, and ischemia-induced neuronal injury.
source: ASIC1a is a proton-gated sodium channel involved in modulation of pain, fear, addiction, and ischemia-induced neuronal injury.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that draws from established scientific knowledge about ASIC1a function.

claim: Cryo-electron microscopy of the human ASIC1a channel at pH 7.4 in complex with Nb.C1 yielded a structure at 2.9 Å resolution.
source: Cryo-electron microscopy of the human ASIC1a channel at pH 7.4 in complex with one of these, Nb.C1, yielded a structure at 2.9 Å resolution.
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental data from cryo-EM studies showing the resolution achieved.

claim: Nb.C1 binds to a site overlapping with that of the Texas coral snake toxin (MitTx1) and the black mamba venom Mambalgin-1.
source: It is revealed that Nb.C1 binds to a site overlapping with that of the Texas coral snake toxin (MitTx1) and the black mamba venom Mambalgin-1
evidence: This is based on structural analysis comparing binding sites in the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The Nb.C1-binding site does not overlap with that of the inhibitory tarantula toxin psalmotoxin-1 (PcTx1).
source: however, the Nb.C1-binding site does not overlap with that of the inhibitory tarantula toxin psalmotoxin-1 (PcTx1).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison of binding sites.

claim: Fusion of Nb.C1 with PcTx1 in a single polypeptide markedly enhances the potency of PcTx1.
source: Fusion of Nb.C1 with PcTx1 in a single polypeptide markedly enhances the potency of PcTx1
evidence: This is supported by functional experiments showing enhanced inhibition.

claim: Competition of Nb.C1 and MitTx1 for binding reduces channel activation by the toxin.
source: whereas competition of Nb.C1 and MitTx1 for binding reduces channel activation by the toxin.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data showing reduced MitTx-induced currents.

claim: ASICs are proton-activated sodium channels present in most neurons of the central and peripheral nervous systems.
source: ASICs are proton-activated sodium channels present in most neurons of the central and peripheral nervous systems (Krishtal and Pidoplichko, 1981; Waldmann et al., 1997).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: There are four ASIC genes (ASIC1-4) and six isoforms in the human genome.
source: There are four ASIC genes (ASIC1-4) and six isoforms in the human genome (Kellenberger and Schild, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: ASIC1a is the most abundant and broadly expressed subunit.
source: The most abundant and broadly expressed subunit is ASIC1a
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: Deletion of ASIC1a in the mouse genome eliminates most of the proton-induced currents mediated by ASICs.
source: its deletion in the mouse genome eliminates most of the proton-induced currents mediated by ASICs (Wemmie et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior experimental work.

claim: Association of three pore-forming subunits, either as homotrimers or heterotrimers, forms functional ASIC channels.
source: Association of three pore-forming subunits, either as homotrimers or heterotrimers, forms functional channels.
evidence: This is established knowledge about ASIC channel structure.

claim: All ASIC isoforms share a common structure consisting of two transmembrane domains (TM1 and TM2), cytosolic amino- and carboxy-termini with the amino-terminus forming a reentrant loop into the lower pore, and a large extracellular domain (ECD) that adopts a fist-like conformation with distinct subdomains.
source: All ASIC isoforms share a common structure consisting of two transmembrane domains (TMDs) (TM1 and TM2), cytosolic amino- and carboxy-termini with the amino-terminus forming a reentrant loop into the lower pore (Yoder and Gouaux, 2020), and a large extracellular domain (ECD) that adopts a fist-like conformation with distinct subdomains.
evidence: This is supported by citations to structural studies.

claim: The first crystal structure of chicken ASIC (cASIC1) was obtained in the desensitized conformation at low pH.
source: These structural features were unveiled by the first crystal structure (Jasti et al., 2007), which was obtained from chicken ASIC (cASIC1) in the desensitized conformation at low pH.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to the original structural study.

claim: Structures of cASIC1 in the open, closed, and desensitized conformations at high and low pH have been resolved.
source: Subsequently, structures of cASIC1 in the open (Baconguis et al., 2014), closed (Yoder et al., 2018), desensitized at high and low pH (Gonzales et al., 2009; Yoder and Gouaux, 2020), and in complex with various toxins have been resolved (Dawson et al., 2012; Baconguis and Gouaux, 2012; Baconguis et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to structural studies.

claim: Structures of hASIC1a have been obtained alone and in complex with Mambalgin-1 toxin.
source: Recently, structures of a human ASIC subunit, hASIC1a, have been obtained alone and in complex with Mambalgin-1 toxin (Sun et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a recent structural study.

claim: PcTx1 is a 40-residue peptide from the venom of the tarantula Psalmopoeus cambridgei that inhibits hASIC1a with IC50 ~3 nM when conditioned at pH 7.2.
source: PcTx1 is a 40-residue peptide from the venom of the tarantula Psalmopoeus cambridgei (Escoubas et al., 2000) that inhibits hASIC1a (IC50 ~3 nM when conditioned at pH 7.2).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: PcTx1 has been investigated as an analgesic and neuroprotective agent from ischemic injury of the brain.
source: It has been investigated as an analgesic and neuroprotective agent from ischemic injury of the brain (Mazzuca et al., 2007; Xiong et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Mambalgin-1 is a 78-residue three-finger toxin from the venom of the black mamba snake Dendroaspis polypepsis that rapidly and reversibly inhibits ASIC1a in neurons.
source: Mambalgin-1 is a 78-residue three-finger toxin from the venom of the black mamba snake Dendroaspis polypepsis that rapidly and reversibly inhibits ASIC1a in neurons (Diochot et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Mambalgin-1 exhibits strong analgesic effects and has raised interest as a potential treatment for chronic pain and as an alternative to opioids.
source: Because Mambalgin-1 exhibits strong analgesic effects, it has raised interest as a potential treatment for chronic pain and as an alternative to opioids (Diochot et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: MitTx, found in the venom of the Texas coral snake Micrurus tener tener, functions as a potent, persistent, and selective agonist for ASICs.
source: Third, the toxin MitTx, found in the venom of the Texas coral snake Micrurus tener tener, functions as a potent, persistent, and selective agonist for ASICs (Bohlen et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: MitTx is a heterodimer of an α-subunit (60 a.a.) and β-subunit (119 a.a.).
source: It is a heterodimer of an α-subunit (60 a.a.) and β-subunit (119 a.a.).
evidence: This is established knowledge about MitTx structure.

claim: ASIC toxins bind primarily to the thumb domain of the ECD of ASICs.
source: These toxins bind primarily to the thumb domain of the ECD of ASICs.
evidence: This is established knowledge from structural studies.

claim: Structures of PcTx1, MitTx, and Mambalgin-1 in complex with cASIC1 have been solved.
source: Structures of each of these toxins in complex with cASIC1 have been solved
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior structural studies.

claim: A cryo-EM structure of hASIC1a bound to Mambalgin-1 at pH 7.4 was solved at 3.9 Å resolution.
source: and in the recent study of hASIC1a by Sun et al., 2020 a cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) structure of hASIC1a bound to Mambalgin-1 at pH 7.4 was solved at 3.9 Å resolution.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a prior structural study.

claim: Nanobodies are derived from the variable domain (VHH) of single-domain antibodies produced in camelids and in cartilaginous fishes.
source: These versatile molecules are derived from the variable domain (VHH) of single-domain antibodies produced in camelids (Hamers-Casterman et al., 1993) and in cartilaginous fishes (Stanfield et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: An alpaca was immunized through the injection of 293 T cells expressing full-length hASIC1a on a 9-week immunization schedule.
source: An alpaca was immunized through the injection of 293 T cells expressing full-length hASIC1a on a 9-week immunization schedule (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure used to generate nanobodies.

claim: Sera collected post-immunization contained conventional IgG1 and single-domain IgG2/3 antibodies that bind to hASIC1a.
source: Sera collected post-immunization contained conventional IgG1 and single-domain IgG2/3 antibodies that bind to hASIC1a, as analyzed by ELISA (Figure 1A–B).
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data shown in the figures.

claim: A phage display library was constructed from mRNA isolated from peripheral lymphocytes with a titer of approximately 10^9 independent clones.
source: A phage display library was constructed from mRNA isolated from peripheral lymphocytes (titer of approximately 109 independent clones) (Pardon et al., 2014; Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–E).
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure and library size achieved.

claim: Three successive panning protocols were used: the first panning was conducted on Xenopus oocytes injected with hASIC1a cRNA while the second and third used recombinant hASIC1a protein bound to agarose and magnetic beads, respectively.
source: To select Nbs that recognize hASIC1a in native conformation and to minimize isolation of nonspecific binders, three successive panning protocols were used: the first panning was conducted on Xenopus oocytes injected with hASIC1a cRNA while the second and third used recombinant hASIC1a protein bound to agarose and magnetic beads, respectively (Figure 1C).
evidence: This describes the experimental screening strategy.

claim: Approximately 200 clones were selected for sequencing of DNA from 600 tested by ELISA.
source: Phagemids recovered from the third panning were used for expression and isolation of Nbs: 600 were tested by ELISA. We considered a clone to be positive if the ELISA intensity was above a threshold that eliminated about two-thirds of the clones. Representative ELISA results are shown in Source data 1. Approximately 200 clones were selected for sequencing of DNA.
evidence: This describes the experimental screening results.

claim: Many of ELISA positive clones were identical or had one or two amino acid differences, which is consistent with efficient enrichment for high affinity clones.
source: The sequencing result indicated that many of ELISA positive clones were identical or had one or two amino acid differences, which is consistent with efficient enrichment for high affinity clones obtained by our screening strategy.
evidence: This is an inference from the sequencing data about the screening efficiency.

claim: DNA sequences of final candidates separated into three main groups.
source: DNA sequences of final candidates separated into three main groups, as shown in a phylogeny tree (Figure 1E) and in the protein alignment of Figure 1—figure supplement 2.
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis of the sequences.

claim: The group consisting of C1-4-5, D10, and H10 produced strong signals and low background in immunofluorescence of cells transfected with hASIC1a.
source: All these clones were further examined by immunofluorescence of cells transfected with hASIC1a. From all the Nbs tested, the group consisting of C1-4-5, D10, and H10 produced strong signals and low background.
evidence: This is based on immunofluorescence experimental data.

claim: A different group (1A-B1, 2B-D4, and 2B-E60) required permeabilization of cells for labeling, suggesting that the recognized epitopes are intracellular.
source: A different group (1A-B1, 2B-D4, and 2B-E60) required permeabilization of cells for labeling, suggesting that the recognized epitopes are intracellular; this was confirmed in immunocytochemistry of permeabilized cells.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental observation that permeabilization was required.

claim: Nb.C1 was added to large-scale preparations of crude membranes from 293 F cells expressing an affinity-tagged construct prior to solubilization with DDM detergent.
source: Subsequently, Nb.C1 was added to large-scale preparations of crude membranes from 293 F cells expressing an affinity-tagged construct (functional hASIC1a comprising amino acids 12–478 with a Strep Tag II in the N-terminus) prior to solubilization with DDM detergent.
evidence: This describes the experimental purification protocol.

claim: After affinity purification, the hASIC1a-Nb.C1 complex was pure and monodispersed.
source: After affinity purification, the hASIC1a-Nb.C1 complex was pure and monodispersed (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by size exclusion chromatography data.

claim: Solubilized hASIC1a alone shows protein aggregates in size exclusion chromatography.
source: This contrasts with the protein aggregates observed in size exclusion chromatography (SEC) of solubilized hASIC1a alone (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by SEC data showing aggregation.

claim: In the complex, proteins from the peak of the SEC showed bands for hASIC1a and Nb.C1 consistent with a stoichiometric ratio of 1:1.
source: In the complex, proteins from the peak of the SEC separated by gel electrophoresis showed bands for hASIC1a and Nb.C1 consistent with a stoichiometric ratio of 1:1 (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is based on gel electrophoresis data.

claim: The structure of hASIC1a-Nb.C1 complex at pH 7.4 was determined with estimated resolution of 2.9 Å.
source: We determined the cryo-EM structure of hASIC1a-Nb.C1 complex at pH 7.4 with estimated resolution of 2.9 Å (Figure 3; Figure 3—figure supplement 1; Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by cryo-EM data and resolution estimation.

claim: hASIC1a is a trimer with each subunit ECD resembling the architecture of a hand.
source: In agreement with other ASIC structures, hASIC1a is a trimer with each subunit ECD resembling the architecture of a hand.
evidence: This is based on the cryo-EM structure and comparison with prior structures.

claim: At pH 7.4 the thumb domain is away from the finger producing an expanded acidic pocket as observed previously in cASIC1 and hASIC1a.
source: At pH 7.4 the thumb domain is away from the finger producing an expanded acidic pocket as observed previously in cASIC1 (Yoder et al., 2018) and hASIC1a (Sun et al., 2020).
evidence: This is based on structural observation and comparison with prior structures.

claim: The TMD shows a closed pore and the domain-swapped TM2 helixes that define the GAS belt of the pore.
source: The TMD shows a closed pore and the domain-swapped TM2 helixes that define the GAS belt of the pore.
evidence: This is based on structural observation from the cryo-EM map.

claim: Protein densities were observed in the EM map inside the lower pore that were weak, presumably from disorder.
source: We also observed protein densities in the EM map inside the lower pore that were weak, presumably from disorder.
evidence: This is an observation from the cryo-EM map with speculation about the cause.

claim: When the map was filtered to 7 Å resolution, density for a reentrant loop with two short helices was observed, consistent with the loop described by Yoder and Gouaux, 2020.
source: When the map was filtered to 7 Å resolution (Figure 3—figure supplement 2) density for a reentrant loop with two short helices was observed, consistent with the loop described by Yoder and Gouaux, 2020.
evidence: This is based on cryo-EM map analysis and comparison with prior structural work.

claim: In cASIC1 the reentrant loops, one from each subunit, form the lower ion permeation pathway.
source: In cASIC1 the reentrant loops, one from each subunit, form the lower ion permeation pathway.
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior structural studies of cASIC1.

claim: In each reentrant loop, the short linker between the helices Re-1 and Re-2 contains the highly conserved HG motif (His28, Gly29) that, in combination with the GAS belt, is involved in channel gating and selectivity.
source: In each loop, the short linker between the helices Re-1 and Re-2 contains the highly conserved HG motif (His28, Gly29) that, in combination with the GAS belt, is involved in channel gating and selectivity.
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior functional and structural studies.

claim: Three Nbs are observed bound to the trimeric channel, each in contact with a subunit at the end of the α4-helix and the extended loop of the thumb domain.
source: Three Nbs are observed bound to the trimeric channel, each in contact with a subunit at the end of the α4-helix and the extended loop of the thumb domain (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is based on structural observation from the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The most noticeable structural difference between hASIC1a and cASIC1 is in the long loop that extends down from the α4-helix to the tip of the thumb.
source: The most noticeable structural difference between hASIC1a and cASIC1 is in this long loop that extends down from the α4-helix to the tip of the thumb (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison between hASIC1a and cASIC1.

claim: The loop is longer and more twisted in hASIC1a because it has two extra amino acids D298 and L299 (DL) that are absent in cASIC1 and in all other known ASIC isoforms.
source: The loop is longer and more twisted in hASIC1a because it has two extra amino acids D298 and L299 (DL) that are absent in cASIC1 and in all other known ASIC isoforms.
evidence: This is based on structural observation and sequence comparison.

claim: The two amino acids D298 and L299 are essential for binding of Nb.C1 as their deletion from hASIC1a eliminates the signal in immunofluorescence microscopy.
source: These two amino acids are essential for binding of Nb.C1 as their deletion from hASIC1a eliminates the signal in immunofluorescence microscopy.
evidence: This is based on mutagenesis and immunofluorescence experiments.

claim: Channels that do not encode D298 and L299 residues such as cASIC1, mASIC1a, mASIC2a, and mASIC3 are not recognized by Nb.C1 in IF experiments.
source: Channels that do not encode those two residues such as cASIC1, mASIC1a, mASIC2a, and mASIC3 are also not recognized by Nb.C1 in IF experiments (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is based on immunofluorescence experiments with different ASIC isoforms.

claim: D296 of hASIC1a interacts with Nb-Y108.
source: Two Asp residues in the extended loop of the thumb are involved: D296 interacts with Nb-Y108
evidence: This is based on structural analysis of the binding interface.

claim: D298 of hASIC1a interacts with Nb-R35 and Nb-R105.
source: and D298 with Nb-R35 and Nb R105.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis of the binding interface.

claim: R317 at the end of α4 of hASIC1a interacts with Nb-F58.
source: In addition, R317 at the end of α4 interacts with Nb-F58.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis of the binding interface.

claim: None of the Nb.C1 interactions would be possible in cASIC1.
source: None of these interactions would be possible in cASIC1.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural comparison and the absence of key residues in cASIC1.

claim: The loop in the hASIC1a structure of Sun et al., 2020 is poorly resolved, but in the current structure is well defined likely because of stabilization provided by Nb.C1.
source: The loop in the hASIC1a structure of Sun et al., 2020 is poorly resolved, but in the current structure is well defined likely because of stabilization provided by Nb.C1, as shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.
evidence: This is based on comparison of structures and speculation about the mechanism of improved resolution.

claim: Nb.C1 binding did not change the channel's properties including average magnitude of current, rate of desensitization, midpoint pH of activation (pH50a), and steady-state desensitization (pH50ssd).
source: Of note, extensive functional analysis of hASIC1a bound to Nb.C1 showed that Nb binding did not change the channel's properties. The average magnitude of current, rate of desensitization, midpoint pH of activation (pH50a), and of steady-state desensitization (pH50ssd) were all unchanged (Figure 3—figure supplement 5A–B).
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological measurements comparing channels with and without Nb.C1.

claim: The presence of the DL motif affects the pH dependence of activation and desensitization.
source: The presence of the DL motif itself, however, affects the pH dependence of activation and desensitization.
evidence: This is based on functional experiments with DL deletion and insertion mutants.

claim: DL lies within a five-amino-acid stretch of hASIC1a which, when mutated, confers the altered pH sensitivity of the mouse isoform on hASIC1a.
source: DL lies within a five-amino-acid stretch of hASIC1a which, when mutated, confers the altered pH sensitivity of the mouse isoform on hASIC1a (Sherwood and Askwith, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior mutagenesis studies.

claim: Deletion of DL in hASIC1a produces a small but significant left shift of the pH50ssd from 7.11±0.02 to 7.18±0.02.
source: Deletion of DL in hASIC1a produces a small but significant left shift of the pH50ssd (from 7.11±0.02 to 7.18±0.02)
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological measurements of the mutant.

claim: Insertion of DL into cASIC1 produces a right shift of pH50ssd from 7.45±0.01 to 7.38±0.01.
source: while insertion of DL into cASIC1 produces the opposite effect (from 7.45±0.01 to 7.38±0.01) (Figure 3—figure supplement 5C–D).
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological measurements of the mutant.

claim: The α-subunit of MitTx interacts with the tip of the thumb close to the membrane bilayer, and with the extended chain that connects α5 to the β10 strand.
source: The superimposition of cASIC1-MitTx1 in the open conformation shows the α-subunit of the toxin interacting with the tip of the thumb close to the membrane bilayer, and with the extended chain that connects α5 to the β10 strand.
evidence: This is based on structural superimposition analysis.

claim: The β-subunit of MitTx forms contacts with α4 and α5 of the thumb, extensively overlapping with the binding site of PcTx1 but not with that of Nb.C1.
source: Meanwhile, the β-subunit forms contacts with α4 and α5 of the thumb, extensively overlapping with the binding site of PcTx1 but not with that of Nb.C1.
evidence: This is based on structural superimposition analysis.

claim: The bulky scaffold of the Nb produces steric hindrance to binding of the α-subunit of MitTx.
source: Though the binding sites of Nb.C1 and MitTx subunits are different, the bulky scaffold of the Nb produces steric hindrance to binding of the α-subunit, marked in the figure by a dashed square.
evidence: This is an inference from structural analysis about potential steric clashes.

claim: Nb.C1 and PcTx1 bind at distinct and well-separated sites, preventing mutual interference when both peptides bind simultaneously to the surface of the channel.
source: In contrast, Nb.C1 and PcTx1 bind at distinct and well-separated sites, preventing mutual interference when both peptides bind simultaneously to the surface of the channel (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is based on structural superimposition analysis.

claim: Mambalgin-1 and Nb.C1 share common interactions: residue D298 of hASIC1 interacts with K8 in Mambalgin-1, and hASIC1 residues at the end of α4 interact with both polypeptides.
source: Mambalgin-1 and Nb.C1 share common interactions: residue D298 of hASIC1 interacts with K8 in Mambalgin-1, and hASIC1 residues at the end of α4 interact with both polypeptides.
evidence: This is based on structural superimposition analysis.

claim: There are clashes between Nb.C1 and Mambalgin-1 that would interfere with simultaneous binding.
source: The dashed square indicates the area of clashes between Nb.C1 and toxin (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is based on structural superimposition analysis showing steric clashes.

claim: The predicted overlap of Nb.C1 with the MitTx α-subunit binding site suggests that Nb.C1 could interfere with the action of MitTx on hASIC1a.
source: The predicted overlap of Nb.C1 with the MitTx α-subunit binding site raises the possibility that Nb.C1 could interfere with the action of MitTx on hASIC1a.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on structural analysis.

claim: MitTx-induced currents were decreased in oocytes pretreated with Nb.C1.
source: To that end, oocytes expressing hASIC1a were incubated with 50 nM of Nb.C1 for 15 min; they were then exposed to 50 nM of MitTx at pH 7.4 while measuring currents with two-electrode voltage clamp. MitTx-induced currents were decreased in oocytes pretreated with the Nb (Figure 5A–D)
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological measurements.

claim: The decrease in MitTx-induced currents is consistent with Nb.C1 interfering with toxin binding to hASIC1a.
source: consistent with the Nb.C1 interfering with toxin binding to hASIC1a.
evidence: This is an inference from the functional data.

claim: PcTx1 functions as an inhibitor of ASIC1a by shifting the steady-state desensitization toward more alkaline pH.
source: PcTx1 functions as an inhibitor of ASIC1a by shifting the steady-state desensitization toward more alkaline pH (Chen et al., 2005; Saez et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior functional studies.

claim: Two crystal structures of cASIC1 with PcTx1 show that the toxin binds to the α5-helix of the thumb, at the interface with the palm domain of the adjacent subunit.
source: Two crystal structures of cASIC1 with PcTx1 show that the toxin binds to the α5-helix of the thumb, at the interface with the palm domain of the adjacent subunit (Dawson et al., 2012; Baconguis and Gouaux, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior structural studies.

claim: The apparent EC50 of PcTx1 for hASIC1a has been reported in the range 0.9–3.7 nM.
source: The apparent EC50 of PcTx1 for hASIC1a has been reported in the range 0.9–3.7 nM
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior functional studies.

claim: The time constant of recovery from PcTx1 inhibition is reported as 125 s or 87 s.
source: and the time constant of recovery from inhibition is reported as 125 s (Chen et al., 2021) or 87 s (Chassagnon et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior functional studies.

claim: Slowing the recovery from PcTx1 inhibition would be advantageous for in vivo applications of PcTx1 either as a potential pain suppressor or for protecting neurons from ischemia of the brain.
source: We hypothesized that slowing the recovery from inhibition would be advantageous for in vivo applications of PcTx1 either as a potential pain suppressor or for protecting neurons from ischemia of the brain.
evidence: This is a hypothesis about potential therapeutic applications.

claim: An Nb.C1-PcTx1 fusion construct produced a fluorescence signal that decorated the plasma membrane of SH-SY5Y cells.
source: To verify binding we first used SH-SY5Y cells, which are derived from a human neuroblastoma and express endogenous hASIC1a (Xiong et al., 2012). An Nb.C1-PcTx1 fusion construct produced a fluorescence signal that decorated the plasma membrane of SH-SY5Y (Figure 5E–G).
evidence: This is based on immunofluorescence data.

claim: Nb.C1 remains bound to the channel with no significant decay through a 4 hr observation period in live cells.
source: Confocal images showed no decay of the Nb.C1 signal during the course of the experiment indicating that the Nb.C1 remains bound to the channel with no significant decay through the 4 hr observation period (Figure 5H–I).
evidence: This is based on time-course immunofluorescence experiments.

claim: From surface plasmon resonance experiments, association rate constants kon ranging from 6.8×10^4 to 2.2×10^5 M^-1 s^-1 were obtained for Nb.C1 binding to hASIC1a.
source: From experiments with two different Nb and hASIC1a protein preparations, global fits to association time courses with Nb concentrations from 0.4 to 100 nM yielded association rate constants kon ranging from 6.8×104 to 2.2×105 M−1 s−1.
evidence: This is based on surface plasmon resonance measurements.

claim: A dissociation rate constant koff ≲ 1.4×10^-5 s^-1 (0.05 hr^-1) can be estimated from the live-cell binding data.
source: Unfortunately, the dissociation time courses (measured for up to 1 hr) from these experiments were too brief to observe the full dissociation time course, but a rate constant koff ≲ 1.4×10−5 s−1 (0.05 hr−1) can be estimated from the live-cell binding data of Figure 5I.
evidence: This is an estimate based on the live-cell binding data.

claim: Taking the smallest kon value as a lower bound on association rate yields the equilibrium constant kd ≲ 0.2 nM.
source: Taking the smallest kon value as a lower bound on association rate yields the equilibrium constant kd ≲ 0.2 nM.
evidence: This is calculated from the measured rate constants.

claim: Cells pre-incubated with PcTx1 recovered current faster (τoff 220 s) and more completely (90 ± 16%) than those pre-incubated with the fusion proteins.
source: Cells pre-incubated with PcTx1 recovered current faster (τoff220 s) and more completely (90 ± 16%) than those pre-incubated with the fusion proteins (Figure 5I–J).
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological measurements.

claim: Cells exposed to Nb.C1-Flex-PcTx recovered only a small fraction of the initial current after 25 min (0.16) with a calculated τoff of 355 s.
source: Cells exposed to Nb.C1-Flex-PcTx recovered only a small fraction of the initial current after 25 min (0.16) even though the calculated τoff (355 s) was not much slower than that of toxin alone
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological measurements.

claim: Nb.C1-Rigid-PcTx reached a lower plateau level (0.14) and slower rate of recovery (τoff = 882 s) compared to the flexible linker.
source: whereas Nb.C1-Rigid-PcTx reached a lower plateau level (0.14) and slower rate of recovery (τoff = 882 s) compared to the flexible linker (Source data 3).
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological measurements.

claim: The partial recovery may be attributed to the presence of some free toxin from cleavage of the fusion proteins and was observed most prominently with the flexible linker.
source: The partial recovery may be attributed to the presence of some free toxin from cleavage of the fusion proteins and was observed most prominently with the flexible linker (Figure 5J).
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism of partial recovery based on gel analysis showing cleavage.

claim: PcTx1 tethered to Nb.C1 significantly potentiates the action of the toxin.
source: Together these experiments indicate that PcTx1 tethered to Nb.C1 significantly potentiates the action of the toxin.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the functional experiments.

claim: Nb.C1 prevents aggregation and stabilizes hASIC1a, markedly improving the quality of the sample preparation for cryo-EM studies.
source: Here, we show that one Nb (Nb.C1) isolated from a phage display library prevents aggregation and stabilizes hASIC1a, markedly improving the quality of the sample preparation for cryo-EM studies.
evidence: This is based on comparison of SEC profiles with and without Nb.C1.

claim: The Nb has potential toward attaining high-resolution structural information of hASIC1a in additional conformations.
source: We obtained the structure of hASIC1-Nb.C1 complex in the closed conformation at 2.9 Å resolution, indicating that the Nb has potential toward attaining high-resolution structural information of hASIC1a in additional conformations.
evidence: This is speculation about future applications based on the current success.

claim: The growing use of Nbs in structural biology stems from the fact that they can stabilize native conformations of proteins, in particular membrane proteins, facilitating structural analysis by crystallization or cryo-EM.
source: The growing use of Nbs in structural biology stems from the fact that they can stabilize native conformations of proteins, in particular membrane proteins, facilitating structural analysis by crystallization or cryo-EM.
evidence: This is general knowledge about nanobody applications in structural biology.

claim: The two extra amino acids D298 and L299 unique to hASIC1a determine the high specificity of Nb.C1 toward hASIC1a.
source: The cryo-EM structure of the hASIC1a-Nb.C1 complex reveals that Nb.C1 binds to the thumb domain of hASIC1a to an epitope in the extended loop of the thumb that contains two extra amino acids (D298 and L299) unique to hASIC1a. These residues determine the high specificity toward hASIC1a and their absence explains the lack of reactivity with other species or isoforms (cASIC1, mASIC1, ASIC2, or ASIC3).
evidence: This is an inference from structural and functional data.

claim: Nb.C1 binding spans to the end of the α4-helix, a region on the surface of the ECD that is also recognized by various toxin polypeptides with functional activity toward many ASIC isoforms.
source: Nb.C1 binding also spans to the end of the α4-helix. This is a region on the surface of the ECD that is also recognized by various toxin polypeptides with functional activity toward many ASIC isoforms.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis and comparison with toxin binding sites.

claim: Nb.C1 could serve as a competitive antagonist to MitTx and as a potential antidote for the pain-producing component of the snake bite.
source: Therefore, Nb.C1 could serve as a competitive antagonist to MitTx and as a potential antidote for the pain-producing component of the snake bite.
evidence: This is speculation about potential therapeutic applications based on the functional data.

claim: Nbs offer practical advantages over currently available antivenoms usually raised in sheep or horses because Nbs can be produced in bacteria in large amounts and at low cost.
source: Nbs offer practical advantages over currently available antivenoms usually raised in sheep or horses (Yang et al., 2017) because Nbs can be produced in bacteria in large amounts and at low cost.
evidence: This is general knowledge about nanobody production advantages.

claim: The lack of competition for binding sites and steric interference but yet close proximity of the Nb.C1 and PcTx1 binding sites offers the possibility of using Nb.C1 as a carrier for PcTx1 to increase potency and decrease off-target effects of the toxin.
source: The Nb.C1-binding site is distinct from that of the inhibitory toxin PcTx. The lack of competition for binding sites and steric interference but yet close proximity of the two binding sites offers the possibility of using Nb.C1 as a carrier for PcTx1 to increase potency and decrease off-target effects of the toxin.
evidence: This is speculation about potential applications based on structural analysis.

claim: A fusion protein incorporating Nb.C1 achieves inhibition of ~84–87% that persists for more than 30 min in functional studies.
source: While the effect of PcTx1 alone is rapidly reversible, a fusion protein incorporating Nb.C1 achieves inhibition of ~84–87% that persists for more than 30 min in functional studies
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological measurements.

claim: The fusion protein remains bound for more than 4 hr on the surface of live cells according to IF assays.
source: and remains bound for more than 4 hr on the surface of live cells according to IF assays.
evidence: This is based on time-course immunofluorescence experiments.

claim: The changes in toxin kinetics are consistent with the Nb having a much slower koff rate than that of the toxin.
source: The changes in toxin kinetics are consistent with the Nb having a much slower koff rate than that of the toxin.
evidence: This is an inference from the functional and binding data.

claim: Further optimization of the sequence of the linker, mainly to minimize or eliminate cleavage, could increase even more the fractional current inhibited by the Nb.C1-PctX fusion peptide.
source: Further optimization of the sequence of the linker, mainly to minimize or eliminate cleavage, could increase even more the fractional current inhibited by the Nb.C1-PctX fusion peptide.
evidence: This is speculation about future improvements based on observed cleavage.

claim: Tethering of PcTx to the Nb would direct the toxin to bind preferentially to the subunit ASIC1a increasing specificity, which is beneficial for in vivo applications such as the amelioration of ischemic damage to the brain.
source: Tethering of PcTx to the Nb also would direct the toxin to bind preferentially to the subunit ASIC1a increasing specificity, which is beneficial for in vivo applications such as the amelioration of ischemic damage to the brain (McCarthy et al., 2015; Yang et al., 2011; Xiong et al., 2004).
evidence: This is speculation about potential therapeutic applications supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Nb.C1 does not interact with the α5-helix of the thumb, while the three toxins in consideration all bind to α5 and these interactions change the conformation of α5 in a toxin-specific manner.
source: We note that Nb.C1 does not interact with the α5-helix of the thumb, while the three toxins in consideration all bind to α5 and these interactions change the conformation of α5 in a toxin-specific manner.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis and comparison.

claim: Many lines of evidence support the notion that displacement of α5 is an essential component of channel gating.
source: Many lines of evidence support the notion that displacement of α5 is an essential component of channel gating.
evidence: This is general knowledge from prior functional and structural studies.

claim: Mutations in α5, formation of cysteine bonds that restrain movement of helix, and binding of polypeptides that produce small but significant displacements are maneuvers that alter gating by lowering pH50a, abolishing currents, inducing desensitization or causing channel opening.
source: Mutations in α5 (Jasti et al., 2007; Vullo et al., 2017), formation of cysteine bonds that restrain movement of helix (Yoder et al., 2018; Chen et al., 2021), and binding of polypeptides that produce small but significant displacements are maneuvers that alter gating by lowering pH50a, abolishing currents, inducing desensitization or causing channel opening.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior functional and structural studies.

claim: The absence of Nb.C1 contacts with α5 is the most likely explanation of why Nb.C1 does not change function of hASIC1a.
source: We posit that the absence of Nb.C1 contacts with α5 is the most likely explanation of why Nb.C1 does not change function of hASIC1a.
evidence: This is an inference from structural and functional data.

claim: Interactions of Nb.C1 are limited to a short segment of the extended loop of the thumb that projects down to TM1 and a segment of the α4-helix of the thumb.
source: Interactions of Nb.C1 are limited to a short segment of the extended loop of the thumb that projects down to TM1 and a segment of the α4-helix of the thumb.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis of the binding interface.

claim: Comparison of the current structure with the hASIC1a structure of Sun et al., 2020 shows that Nb.C1 binding produces a very small movement of α4 and negligible perturbation of α5.
source: Comparison of our structure with the hASIC1a structure of Sun et al., 2020 shows that Nb.C1 binding produces a very small movement of α4 and negligible perturbation of α5 (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison.

claim: SH-SY5Y cells are derived from a human neuroblastoma and express endogenous hASIC1a.
source: To verify binding we first used SH-SY5Y cells, which are derived from a human neuroblastoma and express endogenous hASIC1a (Xiong et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: MitTx is the component of the Texas coral snake venom that produces severe pain by activating hASIC1a in peripheral neurons.
source: This last toxin is the component of the Texas coral snake venom that produces severe pain (Greene et al., 2020) by activating hASIC1a in peripheral neurons (Bohlen et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Most of the binding interference between Nb.C1 and Mambalgin-1 or MitTx α-subunit is due to steric hindrance produced by the scaffold of the Nb, which is large (16.28 kDa) compared to the size of Mambalgin-1 (6.55 kDa) and MitTx α-subunit (7 kDa).
source: In these two instances, most of the binding interference with the Nb is due to steric hindrance produced by the scaffold of the Nb, which is large (16.28 kDa) compared to the size of Mambalgin-1 (6.55 kDa) and MitTx α-subunit (7 kDa).
evidence: This is an inference from structural analysis about the mechanism of interference.
